fields.complete_source: Exercise 13.8. (a) First note that $\mathcal{B}$ is a basis for a topology on $\mathbb{R}$. This follows from the fact that the union of its elements is all of $\mathbb{R}$ and the intersection of two elements of $\mathcal{B}$ is either empty or another element of $\mathcal{B}$. Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$. Clearly the topology generated by $\mathcal{B}$ is coarser than $\mathcal{T}$. Let $U \in \mathcal{T}$ and $x \in U$. Then $U$ contains an open interval with centre $x$. Since the rationals are dense in $\mathbb{R}$ with the standard topology, there exists $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ such that $x \in(x-q, x+q) \subset U$. This proves that $\mathcal{T}$ is coarser than the topology generated by $\mathcal{B}$. We conclude that $\mathcal{B}$ generates the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$.
fields.explanation: The source constructs a rational-radius interval (x-q,x+q) inside U, but this interval need not have rational endpoints and therefore does not itself provide the basis element needed for the reverse-inclusion argument. This is a missing justification in the proof, not a literal false statement of interval containment or a refutation of the topology theorem. Choosing separate rational endpoints around x repairs the argument. The selected Lean declarations prove, for x=√2, q=1/10 and U=(1,2), that x∈(x−q,x+q)⊆U, that both endpoints √2±1/10 are irrational, and that this interval equals no interval with rational endpoints, so it is not a member of B; they do not negate the topology theorem.

fields.problem:
Show that the collection $\{(a,b) \mid a < b, a \text{ and } b \text{ rational}\}$ is a basis that generates the standard topology on $\mathbb{R}$.

DEFINITIONS / CONVENTIONS:
The standard topology on R is the topology generated by the basis of all open intervals (a,b) with a < b real. A basis for a topology on X (Munkres) is a collection B of subsets of X such that every x in X lies in some element of B, and whenever x lies in B1 and B2 in B there is B3 in B with x in B3 subset of B1 intersect B2; the topology generated by B consists of all unions of elements of B. Show the given collection is a basis and that the topology it generates is exactly the standard topology.
